annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygon footprints represent discrete housing association properties/buildings, not a full tessellation. The decisive rule is object/managed asset polygons with numeric attributes, so ObjectDS.
Point features represent discrete archaeological cesspits/finds at addresses; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features mark discrete archaeological finds/locations (waterbed objects) with object codes and captions, so this is a point object layer, not measurements or events.
Polygon features mark discrete archaeological site locations/areas ('vindplaatsen') with names and descriptions, not a full tessellation; classify as bounded objects rather than coverage or amount.
Polygon areas mark selected parks/zones with barbecue restrictions; they are bounded special areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Polygon areas are discrete protected city/townscape zones, not a full tessellation; the decisive rule is ObjectDS for identifiable bounded heritage areas.

Point features mark bee observation locations by area and year; the layer represents identifiable observation sites/species records, not a measurement or event layer. Decisive rule: point objects with categorical attributes -> ObjectDS.
Point layer of honey bee locations where the main mapped phenomenon is numeric abundance (Aantal_volken / number of hives/colonies), so PointDS with AmountDS.
Polygon regions depict a soil quality classification by zone/funktion across selected areas; this is thematic area coverage rather than reporting units, objects, or a full tessellation.
Point features represent individual trees (distinct real-world objects) with attributes like species, planting year, and owner; this is a point object layer, not a measurement or amount layer.
Point features represent individual trees with species, type, owner, and year planted; numeric fields are attributes of objects, so this is an ObjectDS point layer.

Point features represent individual trees (distinct real-world objects) with descriptive attributes like species, height, and planting year; numeric fields are object attributes, not the main mapped quantity.
Point features represent individual trees with identifiers and attributes like species, height, owner, and plant year, so this is an object layer rather than a measurement or amount layer.

Point features mark discrete neighborhood compost locations/initiatives (street names, initiators, start year). Numeric fields are just attributes, so this is an object layer, not an amount or measurement layer.
Polygons mark named camera areas that are discrete bounded zones, not a full tessellation or reporting units; object/zone semantics fit ObjectDS.
Point features represent individual trees (Canadian poplars) with tree IDs and status/management attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features represent individual crowd-monitoring sensors/cameras, i.e. distinct real-world objects; numeric rotation and active flags are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Polygon areas mark selected cultuurhistorische onderzoeksgebieden, not a full tessellation or reporting units; they are bounded phenomenon patches with names and descriptions.
Point layer of knotweed occurrences; each point represents a distinct infestation/object location, with numeric area as an attribute rather than the main mapped phenomenon.
Point layer of ecopassage problem/situation locations; each point represents a discrete barrier/solution site (object) rather than a measurement or event.

Polygon/MultiPolygon areas are discrete selected potential wind-energy zones, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is patch: bounded phenomenon areas with numeric capacity/yield attributes, so not AmountDS.

Point features mark individual voting locations (Stemlocatie/polling stations), and the numeric fields are election attributes rather than the main phenomenon. Classified as object points, not point measurements or amounts.
Point layer of tree-related records (Boom_ID) for oak processionary caterpillar nests; the points represent identifiable objects/trees with attributes, not measurements or events.
Polygon areas depict selected pedicab restriction/permission zones, not a full tessellation or reporting units; the decisive rule is bounded zone/patch rather than coverage or lattice.
Point features represent named standplaatsen (pitches) for pedicabs and coaches, so this is a set of identifiable real-world objects rather than measurements or events.
Point features represent identifiable non-residential premises/addresses with function labels and IDs; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam block/straat units, so geometry is VectorTessellation. The layer maps function mix categories (WON/VZN/WRK and percentages) as an area-wide thematic classification, so CoverageDS.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so geometry is VectorTessellation. The features are reporting/administrative units (buurtcombinaties) with area attributes, which fits LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam; this is a reporting-unit tessellation with area attributes, so LatticeDS.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so the geometry is a tessellation. The layer is an administrative/reporting unit set (buurten) with codes and area, which fits LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so the geometry is a tessellation; they are reporting/statistical units (buurten) with area attributes, so the entity is LatticeDS.
City districts are administrative reporting units forming a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so the geometry is tessellation and the entity is lattice/reporting unit rather than amount.

City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition Amsterdam; the polygons form a near-complete tessellation. The area field is just an attribute, so the decisive rule is reporting unit -> LatticeDS.
Polygon areas form an administrative area partition ('22 Areas') of Amsterdam, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entities are reporting/administrative units.
Administrative area polygons that partition Amsterdam into 22 gebieden; this is a reporting-unit tessellation, with area as an attribute rather than the main phenomenon.
Polygon areas named as Amsterdam practice areas form a near-complete area partition; the decisive rule is reporting-unit tessellation, with area and code fields as attributes.
Polygon regions form a near-complete practice-area partition of Amsterdam; these are reporting/administrative units with area attributes, so use tessellation + lattice.
Polygon areas represent noise contour zones for industrial noise (e.g., 50 dB bands), so this is a contour/interval region layer rather than a tessellation or object layer.
Polygon bands represent noise contour intervals (55-60, 60-65, etc.), so this is a contour/isoline-style region layer rather than a tessellation or object layer.
Polygon regions represent noise contour bands (>70 dB, 65-70 dB, etc.), so this is a contour/interval map rather than reporting units or objects.
Polygon areas represent noise contour bands (50-55 dB, etc.) rather than a full reporting tessellation; decisive rule is contour/interval-band mapping.
Point map of election polling stations (stembureaus/stemlocaties) with vote attributes; the points primarily represent identifiable real-world facilities/places, not measurements or amounts.
Point locations mark individual green roof sites/projects with addresses and roof types; the numeric fields are attributes, so this is an object layer rather than an amount or event layer.
Polygon land-use classification for 2017; the polygons are thematic area classes rather than a full administrative tessellation, so Geometry is PlainVectorRegion and Entity is CoverageDS.
Point features mark individual historical buildings/structures with names and functions; the decisive rule is discrete object points, not amount or event.

The layer shows three bounded municipal polygons, not a full tessellation. The title indicates a ‘how big is Amsterdam’ comparison, and the polygons represent distinct municipal areas/objects rather than a coverage or reporting-unit classification.
Polygon areas for dog off-leash and prohibition zones; these are selected bounded restriction/usage patches, not a full tessellation, reporting unit, or object layer.

Polygon features are discrete named green areas like parks and cemeteries, not a full tessellation or coverage map; classify as bounded objects. Numeric area fields are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point features represent individual private elm trees (a discrete real-world object layer); numeric fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Point locations mark discrete housing projects/buildings with names, owners, and unit counts; the main phenomenon is identifiable real-world objects, not the numeric amount.
Point features represent individual chestnut trees/records; the decisive rule is object points, not amount or event. The status field (aantasting) is an attribute of each tree.

Point features sample a continuous environmental phenomenon; the layer shows drought-related groundwater/ground-level measurements at locations, so PointDS with PointMeasuresDS fits the measurement-layer rule.
Polygon regions show flood risk classes (probability/depth bands), so this is a bounded interval/class map rather than a tessellation or object layer.
Point features represent individual market locations (markets as identifiable places/assets), so geometry is PointDS and the main phenomenon is objects rather than measurements or events.
Point features mark identifiable green monuments/parks/planting sites with names and monument IDs, so this is a point object layer rather than measurements or events.
Point features represent individual monumental trees, a set of identifiable real-world objects; numeric and categorical fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Point layer of identifiable monuments/buildings/assets; the decisive rule is object-by-point, not amount or event. Numeric monument numbers are identifiers, not the main phenomenon.
Point features mark individual wall-plant occurrences/species locations rather than measurements; numeric counts are just attributes, so this is ObjectDS with point geometry.

MultiPolygon features are discrete areas, not a full tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer maps NO2 measurement values over area units with yearly/4-week numeric concentrations, so the main phenomenon is numeric amount (AmountDS), not objects or coverage.
Point locations for NO2 measurement sites; decisive rules are point geometry and sampled environmental measurements at locations.

Polygon regions do not form a full tessellation; the layer appears to show selected gulch areas/patches. The numeric Categorie field is a class attribute, not the main mapped quantity, so PatchDS fits best.
Point layer of soundings/boreholes with measured depths and subsurface values; decisive rule is point measurements of a continuous phenomenon (PointMeasuresDS).
Polygons represent named development neighbourhoods, which are discrete bounded places rather than a full tessellation or thematic coverage; classify as object regions.
Point layer of discrete public toilet locations; the main phenomenon is identifiable facilities/objects, not measurements or events.
Polygon regions mark selected neighbourhoods/areas with overnight-policy conditions; they do not form a full tessellation, so this is a bounded patch layer.
Polygons represent parking-standard category zones, a full-area thematic classification rather than reporting units or discrete objects; decisive rule: coverage.
Polygon features depict discrete named parks/green spaces, not a full tessellation; the decisive rule is bounded real-world objects (parks) with area as an attribute, so ObjectDS.
Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units that partition the city, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is LatticeDS rather than AmountDS; Opp_m2 is just an attribute.
Polygon postcode areas form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam; this is a reporting-unit tessellation, with postcode and area attributes as supporting fields.

Postcode6-vlakken BAG are postcode area polygons that form a near-complete partition, so the geometry is a tessellation. They are reporting/statistical units identified by postcode and buurt codes, so LatticeDS.
LineString features represent road/infrastructure links; the title and attributes (fiets, tram, bus, auto, max speed) indicate a connected transport network, so NetworkDS.

Polygon features are discrete bounded pedestrian areas; the layer represents named/place-like objects (parks/squares) rather than a full tessellation or coverage. The decisive rule is object over amount/coverage.
Point features with location names indicate distinct real-world objects/facilities (masts/locations), not measurements or events.
Point features represent distinct privacy-related research items/cases rather than measurements or events, so this is a point object layer.
Point features represent specific car fleet scan locations/measurement sites with names and addresses, so this is a set of identifiable objects rather than amounts or events.
Point layer of 750 voting locations/polling sites with place names and election results; the main feature is identifiable objects (stemlocaties), not the numeric amounts themselves.

Polygons appear to be area units tied to locations, and the map classifies drainage as possible/not possible. This is a tessellated area layer with Boolean presence/absence style meaning, so ExistenceDS fits best.

Polygon areas are discrete hydro units rather than a full tessellation, so geometry is PlainVectorRegion. The layer represents selected rainproof solution areas/zones for intervention, which fits PatchDS rather than reporting units or coverage.

Polygon areas mark rainproof bottleneck zones (selected affected areas), not a full tessellation or reporting units; this fits PatchDS. Geometry is polygonal but discrete regions, so PlainVectorRegion.
Discrete polygon features with named locations indicate bounded infrastructure sites rather than a tessellation or area-wide coverage; the decisive rule is object/managed site representation.
Point features mark identifiable religious buildings/locations (churches, mosques, temples, centers) with names and addresses, so this is a point object layer rather than amounts or events.
Line geometries representing sidewalk segments along streets; this is a connected infrastructure/route system, so NetworkDS with LineDS.
Line geometry with route/street segments for mopeds on roadways; this is a connected transport/infrastructure network, not isolated objects or amounts.
Point features representing discrete public sports facilities/playgrounds; the numeric Oppervlak is just an attribute, so this is an ObjectDS point layer.
Point locations for city farming sites; each feature is a distinct real-world place/facility with name, address, status, and website, so ObjectDS.
Polygons represent named city farming sites/parks with addresses and websites, so these are discrete bounded objects rather than a tessellation or patch.
Point features represent discrete city pilot initiatives/activities with names, sectors, and years; decisive rule is point objects, not a numeric amount layer.
LineString features represent Amsterdam major streets, which are a connected route/infrastructure system; numeric line numbers are just identifiers, so the decisive rule is network.
Line geometries representing district heating/cooling transport infrastructure; decisive rule is network/route system.

Polygon areas represent district heating/cooling network project zones, not a full tessellation. The decisive rule is network: the layer maps connected utility infrastructure areas/status rather than objects, coverage, or amounts.

Polygon regions mark selected strategic housing-planning areas rather than a full tessellation; they are bounded project/zone patches with attributes like project name and max dwellings, so PatchDS fits better than lattice or coverage.
Point features represent distinct local farms/shops/food venues with names, addresses, products, and flags; this is a point object layer, not a measurement or amount layer.
LineString features represent tram and metro route infrastructure; decisive rule is network/route system, not numeric attributes.
LineString features represent tram and metro routes; the decisive rule is network infrastructure, not numeric attributes.
Point features representing tram stops and metro stations; the decisive rule is object points, not amount or event. Numeric fields are just attributes of the stop objects.
Point geometry with named tram stops and metro stations; the decisive rule is object/facility mapping rather than amount or event. Numeric RADIUS is just an attribute.
Point features represent distinct traffic light/intersection objects, not measurements or events. Numeric fields are identifiers and dates, so the decisive rule is object points.
Line features labeled as road links with traffic forecast volumes (etmaal and modal counts); this is a route/network layer with numeric magnitude as the main phenomenon, so LineDS + AmountDS.
Point layer of election polling/stem locations; each point is a distinct voting location object, with vote totals as attributes rather than the main phenomenon.
Point geometry with one feature per tree; the layer is about identifiable tree objects (‘Tree replacement’), not a measurement or event, so ObjectDS fits best.
Point features are individual traffic information system devices (cameras, displays, sensors) at named standplaatsen; this is a set of identifiable objects, not a measurement or event layer.
Point layer of discrete traffic information system installations (BFA units/pollers/barriers) with IDs and site names, so the decisive rule is object-in-points rather than amounts or events.

Point features mark individual breeding bird locations/nests tied to streets and addresses; main phenomenon is discrete bird sites, not point measurements or amounts. Numeric Aantal fields are attributes, so ObjectDS.
Point features represent individual park benches in Vondelpark, so this is a discrete object layer; the numeric Rotatie field is only an attribute, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Line features represent street segments/straatvakken in a connected walking network; the walkability labels are attributes of that network, so NetworkDS with LineDS.
Point geometry with each feature representing a distinct wall art object at a specific address; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Polygon areas classify the city into welstand (building style) categories; this is an exhaustive area-wide thematic coverage, not reporting units or selected patches.
Polygon layer of Amsterdam building typology/system areas; the polygons classify the full area into thematic categories, so it is a coverage map rather than reporting units or selected patches.
Point locations with dates and descriptions of WWII attacks/incidents; the decisive rule is event, not amount or object.
Polygon features represent discrete housing development projects/sites with project names and phase/year/unit counts; these are bounded project objects, not a full tessellation or amount map.
Point features represent identifiable self-build plot projects/locations, not measurements or events; numeric fields are just attributes, so ObjectDS.

Polygon footprints form discrete roof areas rather than a tessellating reporting layer; the key field is a categorical classification of solar-panel suitability/heritage coverage across those areas, so CoverageDS fits best.

Point features mark solar panel locations on buildings/objects; numeric fields are attributes (panel count, power), not the main phenomenon. Classified as point objects rather than amount or measures.
Point features represent named swimming locations/facilities and bathing places; this is an object layer, not measurements or events.
